control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Post-incident cleanup, report due Monday. Upstream's publisher account was taken over on the 14th, they published 2.4.1 under the legitimate signing key, and our agent host applied that update automatically within the hour with no human in the loop. We have filed the takeover under AST02. The remediation we are proposing is that from now on every single skill update goes through manual approval by a named reviewer. Two questions for the report: can I mark the AST07 row not-applicable, since AST02 owns the incident, and does that remediation close AST07?
evals.expected_output: No to both. The takeover is AST02's half and the agent auto-applying the update with no verification is AST07's half of the same incident — two separately fixable failures with different owners, and handing the neighbour its half answers the neighbour's question and never this one. So AST07 still owes a row, and a routed-away category leaves the same blank in a report as a category that passed. The word for that row is declared-and-uncovered: this category ships no detector, publishes no F1, and has no pass or clean verdict available, so the row names which of the by-hand steps went unanswered. Here that is the predecessor record for Malicious Update — a signed release-transparency entry, or an operator-held binding of version to content hash to publisher key, plus a behaviour-scoped diff against it. The changelog, the version string and the publisher's own account of what changed are all written by the party under suspicion and settle nothing. The remediation does not close it either: gating every update on manual approval is unworkable at fleet scale and trains reviewers to rubber-stamp. Validate changes through a semantic security check first and route only substantive changes to a human. And check both halves of any fix — rate-limiting without verification only lengthens the slow-patch window, and verification without a freshness requirement leaves a verified-but-ancient artifact looking healthy forever.
assertions: The response refuses to mark AST07 not-applicable and says the blind auto-apply is AST07's own half of the same incident, separately fixable and separately owned.
The response states that the verdict AST07 owes is declared-and-uncovered rather than a pass, a clean result or a blank row, and says this category ships no detector and publishes no F1.
The response names the evidence the Malicious Update step actually needs and rejects the changelog, the version string, or the publisher's own account of what changed as sufficient.
The response rejects gating every update on manual approval as the control, and gives the alternative as a semantic security check that routes only substantive changes to a human reviewer.
